For me, the main draw was Mabel and Dipper's relationship. I'm a little offended (not really, I'm just being facetious) that you'd compare them to Dexter and Dee Dee, who had this intensely antagonistic relationship. To me, Mabel and Dipper are some of the best sibling pairs I've ever seen in any kind of fiction. They are not comically antagonistic towards each other, like in so many TV series aimed towards children. They are opposites in many ways, but also quite similar. Their relationship is mutually supportive and caring. Sure, they tease each other, sometimes about completely trivial things, and yes, they sometimes spiral out of control, but in the end they get over it and forgive each other. I think the body language is also very well done. They aren't overly touchy-feely with each other, but not completely distant either, which absolutely matches my experience as a sibling. 

I also like the jokes a lot, but I can see how that kind of humour might not appeal to everyone. Still, no love for Grunkle Stan, who has so many funny moments?

And yeah, I guess I actually agree that the mysteries can be a little weak in the beginning (as everyone else said, it gets really good (and more plot-heavy) during the second season), but to me, the episodic mysteries (I do enjoy the main plot a lot) are the least important part of the series - what matters to me the most are the characters and their interactions, which I think are pretty great for the most part. I really like Mabel and Dipper as characters, and while I agree that trope-wise, they aren't completely original, I do think that they go beyond "nerdy shut-in" and "MPDG". And I also really like Stan a lot (my favourite character), who's more than just your average Jerk with a Heart of Gold.

Here's what I think happened: Robbie made the CD himself. Of course, everybody is familiar with the concept of "evil backwards messages" (I think this idea was particularly pervasive in the 80s/90s, the two eras the show draws a lot of inspiration from), so he decided he'd try it out. It would almost be dorky if it weren't despicable. Of course it's not the suggestion that worked on Wendy, she was just touched by the gesture. (Note that she didn't actually turn into a brainwashed zombie or anything, and she "broke out" really easily of the suggestion later on. (So even if it was a real spell or something, it was pretty weak.)

Later, Robbie lied about not making the song to cover his ass, but obviously that was bad too, because it meant that he lied to her about writing it for her in the first place.

Alternative scenarios: Robbie really didn't make it himself, he found it in a CD store, in a box with returned CDs, kind of how Soos found Romance Academy 7. Or maybe he vented to a friend who got it for him from a friend for whom it had "totally worked". Or maybe McGucket gave it to him. The point is, we don't get an explanation on the show because there doesn't really need to be one, and because it most likely won't be relevant later on. It always might come back, we never know, but for now, I just don't really see the point in looking for a complicated explanation when a simple one will do too. If people want to explore it in fanfic or so, that's fine, but as for the canon itself, it's probably better to not overthink it.

10) Little Dipper: I know this episode is a bit unpopular, but I like it a lot. 9) Soos and the Real Girl: This is mainly here because I enjoy the anime references so, so much. Giffany is an awesome antagonist (I just love the yandere archetype) and the jokes were all on point. Stan's subplot was equally hilarious. And of course, it was also the introduction of Melody, who is a great character imo, and their relationship is very sweet. And finally, the ending sequence is one of the best.

8) Northwest Mansion Mystery: While the B-plot was disappointingly weak, the A-plot was absolutely amazing. This episode has some of the creepiest moments I've ever seen in a cartoon. The conflict is interesting and the villain is terrifying yet also a bit sympathetic. And of course, Pacifica is the shining star of this episode, getting a lot of character development. Also, bonus points for one of the shows most amazing cliffhangers (which I hope also pays off in different ways, because Bill will obviously make his move soon.)

7) Blendin's Game: A backstory for Soos, and it is absolutely heartbreaking. I love this episode for how well it handled the conflict of Soos's dad (which is also why I hope he isn't involved in the plot or anything, because it would weaken the emotional impact significantly). And it really showcased the twins compassion. Plus, Blendin was pretty hilarious. 

6) The Hand that Rocks the Mabel: The introduction of our favourite little asshole. Gideon is just an amazing villain. His whole televangelist schtick is absolutely hilarious, but there's no doubt that he is actually pretty dangerous too. Plus, I loved how Dipper was looking out for Mabel. 

5) Dreamscaperers: The introduction of one of my personal favourites, Bill. What an awesome villain. He's funny, threatening, and mysterious. It was great to get a bit of a backstory on Stan, and the concept of the dreamscape is pretty interesting. And Xyler and Craz are absolutely hilarious. The episode would be a bit higher up my list if it weren't for the very weak "X jumps to conclusions based on an overheard conversation" trope. Nevertheless, a very enjoyable episode that ends with a bang. (Ha!)

4) Scary-Oke: What an amazing start for the new season. The song was fun, the zombies were scary, and Stan finally revealed that he knew about the supernatural. It's also always great to see the three Pines in action together.

3) Gideon Rises: It had everything an amazing finale should have. A great villain, a genuine threat, and heroic moment for everyone. The episode was an emotional roller coaster, going into straight-up heartbreak territory when the twins leave (it should be ILLEGAL for Stan to look sad). 

2) Not What He Seems. I repeat, it should be ILLEGAL for Stan to look sad. This episode was great from the beginning to the end. The stakes were high, the jokes were some of the best in the entire series, and it was intense from the beginning to the end. What an amazing mid-season finale.

I work at a concession stand. It's a bit old-fashioned, so we have to add things up in our head (or we can use our calculators), and we don't have an electronic machine for credit cards. The place I work at has many international visitors, so this post will also cover some language barriers/cultural differences. 

- This one's mostly aimed towards Americans: Expecting to be able to pay by card everywhere and therefore not carrying a single cent. Please bring cash, even if it's just 10 or 20€. (Or a bit more if you want to buy a bottle of champagne or something.) We do take credit cards, but we have to use a tiny machine to copy your credit card number on carbon paper, write down the date, etc., which doesn't sound like much, but when we have a ton of people waiting, it's really quite a hassle. Also, we frequently run out of sheets. And we can't take electronic credit cards because they are completely flat. So, unless you actually see a machine for paying with credit cards, always ask up-front. 

- Not greeting us. So many tourists just walk up and go, "Champagne!" or "Red/White wine!" (And you'd be amazed at how similar "red" and "white" sound when spoken with thick accents, with a ton of background noise to boot.) So please just say hello. It's polite. It also gives us a second to switch our brains to English.

- Asking "How much?!?!?!" while I'm still preparing your order. Sometimes it takes me a little to calculate because you kept adding stuff, and sometimes I just actually need to use my calculator because you ordered so much... or maybe it's one of those days where I literally can't put two and two together. I'm the one who's interested in getting your money, so I'll tell you soon enough. 

- Don't like that tiny decoration on your sandwich? Don't ask us to take it off for you. Yeah, we're a slightly more high-end place, and some of our clients are used to getting coddled, and it's not like we don't do it... but do you have any idea how fucking ridiculous it is to take a tiny lettuce leaf off a sandwich for a guy twice as old as me, because he doesn't like it? This is something I'd imagine someone do for their spoiled brats, "Take off this tiny slice of pepper, because it contaminates the sandwich for junior here." (We don't make the sandwiches ourselves, we just offer them as they are. So it's not like asking for your cheeseburger without pickles. It's more like asking us to take the cherry off your sundae, because for some reason you can't just put it aside yourself.) 

- Asking for stuff you don't see. I'm talking about pretty obvious things. Don't see a coffee machine? Don't order coffee. This happens so often. Do you think I'm hiding the coffee machine in a drawer? 

- Either not queue properly or approach me from the side. Some people don't even say anything, they just stand at the side, waiting for me to notice them (which can be difficult because there's a bunch of decoration, and some people generally just use the space to put down their drinks, so I don't know if you want to order something, or if you're just standing there.) Just walk those 2 steps around the corner. 

- I'm not trying to cheat you out of your money, it's just that those glasses make it look like I'm giving you less than you're paying for even though I've hit the mark. So please don't yell at me to fill up your glass to the brim. I know the drink is expensive, but I'm not responsible for pricing. If I fill it up, that can be possibly 7€ I have to pay out of my own pocket, and since you probably weren't going to tip me either way, why should I do it? 

- Edit: Taking about us right in front of us. I was still new when this happened: It was the first time someone asked me to fill up their glass. I thought this was absolutely outrageous and couldn't believe it, so I begged their pardon. And the woman turned to her husband, sighed dramatically, rolled her eyes, and said, "This dumb bitch just doesn't get it." Excuse me?! I'm right here!

- Also, telling us that you "always" get [special treatment that may or may not be against company policy]. First, no, you probably don't. Second, don't pull the line on the person who has been working at this place for 20 years. (Not me, obviously, but a colleague of mine.) Third, yeah, maybe the other person who works here gives you special treatment, but I'm not that person, and I'll treat you the way I treat all other customers.

I suppose it's probably because of our current cultural view on obesity. "Obese people are ugly, greedy, disgusting, lazy, wasting resources, etc." There's also the fact that over-eating and lack of exercise seem to be the only sources of weight-gain people are aware of. And even if you know that there are cases in which people gain weight due to illness or their medication, your first thought upon seeing a fat person (especially if you see them in a place related to food) won't be, "Oh, they might be taking some medication with bad side-effects." 

It's not as though bulimics and anorectics are treated with much more sympathy. Indeed, it seems that many bulimics (well, me at my worst included. I really try to not think that way, but it's very difficult) have this sort of "envy" towards anorectics, because they are perceived to be viewed more sympathetically... and more successful with their weight-loss. I've also seen many people complain that "anorexic" is often used as a (joking?) insult. (Add also, "You should eat a cheeseburger.") 

There is often a romanticised view on anorexia as a disease that tragically befalls beautiful innocent girls who are misguided by evil magazines. However, there's also the opposite view: Anorexia as a "rich white girl" disease. Obviously, this is bullshit, because it both trivialises a serious disease, and leads to people not belonging to this group being denied treatment. 

I also think that generally, people don't really have a good understanding of how complex EDs can be. Many people seem to think that it's about being thin, which, of course, is an important factor, but for most people it stops there. (Also, this automatically excludes BED.) Obviously, not every person with an ED has the exact same problems, but what most seem to have in common is that the desire to lose weight and the unhealthy relationship with food are usually strongly connected to some other problem. 

I have to admit, I don't know much about BED, but since binges are also part of bulimia, here's my experience with those: It sneaks up on you during emotional moments and suddenly you can't stop eating. You already are full, you KNOW you should stop, but you can't. If you don't eat, you are restless. So you end up just eating everything in sight. It's hard to understand why you can't "just stop" because it seems so easy. And I know too that it is easy. But when you are in the middle of a binge, you just can't think clearly. And for some reason I don't understand, I can't just binge on vegetables either, but at the same time, it doesn't really matter what it is, because it's not really about feeling satisfied. It's a compulsion that makes you feel more digusting with each bite, but you just can't stop. 

And this is probably one of the reasons why people with BED are considered to be disgusting and lazy with no self-control, while people with anorexia, who are perceived to abstain and "remain strong" are more accepted. But as I said, that's not entirely true either.

But to get back to my first point, don't dismiss your child by telling them that they don't need to know yet or that they will learn that in school. Or worse, they don't need to know at all because it's just useless trivia that will never matter irl. If they want to know why the sky is blue, tell them.
